source.title: Brain development during adolescence: neuroscientific insights into this developmental period

confidence_rationale: Independent (German) review corroborating the sensory-first / executive-last ordering and hitting INV-064's most specific behavioural prediction head-on: maximum gray-matter density is reached first in primary sensorimotor cortex and last in prefrontal cortex, while subcortical limbic/reward systems mature earlier, producing a mature-subcortical / immature-PFC imbalance that accounts for adolescent risk-taking persisting past sensory-motor competence. Held to 0.66 because it is a general-audience synthesis (not primary data), the imbalance model is one dominant account among competitors, and it documents ordering + behavioural correlate rather than the necessity claim.
failure_signatures: The mature-subcortical / immature-PFC imbalance is the dominant but not the only account of adolescent risk-taking (pure incentive-processing and social-context accounts compete). If risk-taking is driven mainly by incentive salience independent of the maturational lag, INV-064's specific 'risk-taking persists past sensory-motor competence BECAUSE E3 is still integrating' reading loses this support.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In postnatal human brain development the maximum density of gray matter is reached first in the primary sensorimotor cortex and the prefrontal cortex matures last; subcortical areas, especially the limbic and reward systems, develop earlier, so during adolescence there is an imbalance between more mature subcortical areas and less mature prefrontal areas, which may account for typical adolescent behaviour patterns including risk-taking. The high plasticity of the adolescent brain lets environmental influences exert particularly strong effects on cortical circuitry.
mapping.ree_translation: Independent corroboration of INV-064's ordering (sensorimotor E1/E2 mature before executive E3) plus a direct match to its flagship prediction: risk-taking persists well past sensory-motor competence precisely because the executive layer (PFC / E3) is still integrating while the sensory and subcortical substrates are already mature. The environmental-sensitivity point also supports INV-064's prediction that early high-entropy experience has outsized, lasting effects.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Review-level human evidence, and a general-medical-audience synthesis rather than primary data. The subcortical-cortical imbalance model is the dominant but not the sole account of adolescent risk-taking. Documents ordering and a behavioural correlate, not the necessity / curriculum-causality that is INV-064's strong claim. Sensorimotor -> E1/E2 and PFC -> E3 is a functional analogy.
mapping.source_context: Narrative review of structural and functional human neurodevelopment during adolescence (Deutsches Arzteblatt International, selective PubMed synthesis). Human data; REE transfer by functional analogy.

confidence_components.notes: Reputable peer-reviewed review but general-audience synthesis, not primary data. Mapping fidelity good -- it hits the exact risk-taking-past-competence prediction INV-064 makes. Transfer risk moderate. Provides independent (non-Sydnor-lab) corroboration of the ordering.
